summary.text: El Niño is the warming phase of the El Niño–Southern Oscillation, a pattern of changing sea surface temperatures over the tropical Pacific Ocean.
It builds as weaker easterly trade winds let warm surface water surge east, which weakens the winds even more in a positive feedback.
El Niño events cause short spikes in global average surface temperature, and with La Niña they can bring intense storms in some places and droughts in others.

facts.label: Name meaning
facts.value: 'The Boy' in Spanish, after the Christ Child

facts.label: Why that name
facts.value: The warm current typically appeared around Christmas

facts.label: How often
facts.value: Irregularly, about every two to seven years

facts.label: Air pressure pattern
facts.value: High over Indonesia, low over the East Pacific

items.prompt: The easterly trade winds along the equatorial Pacific grow weaker. What happens to the warm water at the ocean surface?

options.label: It piles up further to the west
It surges toward the east
It sinks into the deep ocean
It stays exactly where it was

items.explain: Weaker easterly trade winds result in a surge of warm surface waters to the east and less upwelling on the equator.

items.prompt: Once El Niño starts, warmer sea water weakens the trade winds, and the weaker winds warm the sea even more. What kind of process is this?

options.label: A negative feedback
An external forcing
A random fluctuation
A positive feedback

items.explain: In the Bjerknes feedback, atmospheric changes alter sea temperatures, which in turn alter the winds, reinforcing the original change.

items.prompt: Why did Peruvian sailors give a warm ocean current the name 'El Niño'?

options.label: It usually showed up around Christmas
It was small and weak, like a young boy
A boy on a fishing boat first spotted it
It came back each year like a birthday

items.explain: Sailors named the warm, south-flowing current after the Christ Child because it typically appeared around Christmas.

items.prompt: A strong El Niño develops this year. What would you expect global average surface temperature to do over the following year or so?

options.label: Dip for a short time
Stay almost unchanged
Spike up for a short time
Step up permanently

items.explain: El Niño events cause short-term spikes, about a year long, in global average surface temperature.

items.prompt: Which country is likely to be hit hardest by El Niño and its cycle?

options.label: A wealthy European country living mostly on services
A developing Pacific country relying on farming and fishing
A desert country with no coastline on any ocean
A rich Pacific country relying on technology exports

items.explain: The countries most affected by ENSO are developing countries bordering the Pacific that depend on agriculture and fishing.

items.prompt: During El Niño, the warm water stored in the western tropical Pacific gets used up. What happens next?

options.label: The warming becomes permanent
The trade winds vanish for good
The warm phase moves to the Atlantic
Conditions go back to normal

items.explain: Once the warm waters in the western tropical Pacific are depleted enough, conditions return to normal.
